prize_parts.citation: for transforming the measurement of intergenerational mobility with population-scale administrative data, and for credible evidence on how neighbourhoods and childhood environments shape economic opportunity

statement.case_for: B002 changed what economists can observe. Linking population-scale administrative records produced geographic mobility maps and quasi-experimental estimates of neighbourhood and childhood-exposure effects, and it set a new empirical standard in labour and public economics. The work is also transparent and checkable. Large samples, explicit designs and findings extended with other administrative datasets make it more robust to the problems that undermine small-sample results, and that matters to me given my metascience background. Its influence on research and policy debate is very large. My reading of the opening evidence is that B002 has the broadest first-place and top-three support, but I do not treat that as scientific merit. I rely on the substance: new facts, credible designs and wide adoption. Chetty, Hendren and Friedman are the natural unit, since they lead the mobility and place-effects papers and the data construction.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and the strength of identification. Most core results are from about 2014 to 2022, so long-run confirmation is not yet available. Causal readings of place effects and extrapolation of exposure effects rest on strong assumptions, and small-area estimates can be noisy. A committee could also see the contribution as mainly empirical measurement rather than a conceptual advance. Credit is spread across a large team, and the three-name cap leaves out Katz, who is credited on the ballot.

responses.point: B002 may be premature relative to the other candidates, since the core work is about a decade old and replication and long-term follow-up are still accumulating. He also notes that credit within a large team is hard to divide.
responses.response: I take the timing concern seriously, and it is my main uncertainty. I weigh it differently, though. The relevant question is whether the central facts and designs have been tested, not how many years have passed. The mobility and exposure-effect findings have been extended and checked with other administrative datasets, and the designs are transparent enough for others to probe. That is a stronger position than a decades-old result resting on a few small lab samples. I agree that the causal place-effect claims deserve caution, and I would keep the citation focused on measurement and on credible evidence about opportunity, not on policy prescriptions. On team credit, the Chetty-Hendren-Friedman trio is the tightest unit, because it corresponds to the lead authorship of the mobility and place-effects papers.

responses.point: He ranks B002 seventh as high and rising but less mature than the others. Recency makes it hard to tell whether the findings will prove foundational, and he adds that Chetty's wider oeuvre, including the B037 tax work, might be judged instead of one narrow discovery.
responses.response: I agree that the oeuvre question is real, but it argues for a precise citation, not against the candidate. The mobility-and-opportunity contribution is a distinct, shortlisted achievement and can be defined narrowly. The B037 tax work is not on this shortlist, so I do not rely on it. On whether the findings will last, a data-and-design contribution has a particular kind of durability. Even if specific estimates are revised, the administrative-data standard and the measurement framework remain. I also grant your point that the older macro candidates have far longer track records, and I would not claim B002 beats them on maturity. My case is that its combination of influence, credibility of design and checkability outweighs the shorter record.

responses.point: She ranks B002 first and sees a strong case under common criteria, but notes that limiting the award to three requires leaving out Katz. She also asks how credit should divide between data infrastructure and the conceptual or causal contributions.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and with the Katz difficulty. His Moving to Opportunity work is a real input, and the ballot does credit him. Three is the maximum for a prize part, though, and Chetty, Hendren and Friedman account for the mobility atlas and exposure-effect papers that define the discovery. I would let the citation do the work on your second question by naming both the measurement advance and the credible evidence on neighbourhood effects. That way the prize does not reward data access alone. If the Committee thought Katz's contribution decisive, I would want to hear that argued on the evidence, not assumed, because swapping him in would change the discovery being rewarded toward the experimental strand.

uncertainties: How much of the neighbourhood and exposure-effect evidence will survive long-run follow-up, and how sensitive it is to identifying assumptions and noise in small-area estimates.
Whether the Committee will treat the contribution as sufficiently conceptual rather than primarily empirical measurement.
Whether Katz's exclusion under the three-name cap is the right call, and how credit should be divided across a large collaborative team.

How the closeness in time and theme to recent prizes on technology, growth and institutions might affect the Committee's appetite for another labour and public economics award. My assessment rests on general knowledge and not on independent verification of citations.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for B002. None of Chetty, Hendren, Friedman or Katz appears among my listed co-authors or networks. My field is behavioural and experimental economics and metascience, which is close to my alternative B001, but the profile lists no co-authorship with the B001 credited names.
